text:
Verses 83–102

Introduction & Commentary

These verses tell the story of Dhū l-Qarnayn and contain one of the Qur’an’s heroic tales.

(18:83) And they ask you about Dhū l-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you an account (dhikran) of him.

This means they ask about Dhū l-Qarnayn’s exploits. The evidence of that is the answer to the question which describes his exploits, but do not acquaint us with his personal details. It even stops at mentioning him by his nickname without going on to state his real name.

Dhikr is either:

1) A verbal noun meaning the object (that is, madhkūr), rendering a meaning of, Say: I will recite to you something worth mentioning (shayʾan madhkūran) about him, that is, about Dhū l-Qarnayn; or, 2) It means the Qur’an—God called it dhikr in many places. Based on that interpretation, it would all mean, “Say: I will recite to you some Qur’an of him”.

Minhu either means (something) about Dhū l-Qarnayn or, (something) from God. It consists of what follows this verse from, Surely We established him in the land, right to the end of the story. The second interpretation (that is, that dhikr means some Qur’an) is more likely.

(18:84) Surely We established (makkanna) him in the land and granted him means of access to everything.

The word tamkin means facilitating. One can either say makkantuhu (I enabled him) or makkantu lahu (I facilitated for him). Tamakkun in the land means the power to dispose of it as he wishes and wants through being made sovereign over it.

It may be claimed that it is derived from makan based on the mistaken belief that the (letter) mim is not one of the root letters. Based on this interpretation, tamkīn would mean giving stability and firmness such that it is not moved from its place by any competing impediment.

A sabab is a link and means. Thus granting him a sabab of everything means giving him some of everything he uses and benefits from,

for example intellect, knowledge, religion, strength, body, abundance of money, soldiers, vastness of dominion, the (ability) to administrate well (ḥusn al-tadbīr) and so on to achieve important life goals. This is a blessing from Him bestowed upon Dhū l-Qarnayn and the great importance

of his affair [is given] with the most eloquent explanation. What He says about his career, deeds, and utterances is full of wisdom and strength which is testimony to that.

(18:85) So he followed a course (fa-atbaʿa sababan).

Itbāʿ means following a course and taking a path toward the place where the sun sets.

(18:86) Until (ḥattā), when he reached the place where the sun set, he found it going down into a black sea, and found by it a people. We said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn! you either give them a chastisement or do them a benefit.

The word ḥattā indicates an implied verb, that is, So he traveled, until, when he reached . . . The phrase, where the sun set, means the western edge of civilization at that time as evidenced by what follows, and found by it a people.

People say that ʿayn ḥamiʾa means an sea of black mud and that ʿayn means sea. Finding the sun setting in a black sea means a place at the sea shore beyond which there is no expectation of there being any more land. So he thought that the sun set in the sea because it was correct to say that it was the horizon. The description of this black sea applies to the Mediterranean. There are eternal islands in it which used to be sources of longevity but they subsequently sank.

An alternative recitation is fiiʿaynin ḥāmiyya, that is, a hot sea. That is true of the points in the Mediterranean close to the equator and near Africa. It may be that Dhū l-Qarnayn reached the shores of Africa on his journey to the west.

We said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn!: When the Qur’an says that He is saying something, it means revelation to a Prophet or communication via revelation, for example: And We said: O Adam! Dwell you . . . (2:35) And when

We said: Enter this city . . . (2:58).

It is also used for inspiration other than to a prophet, for example: And We revealed to Moses’ mother, saying: Nurse him . . . (28:7).

Thus, it is clear that the words, We said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn!, does not mean that he was a prophet who received revelation because God’s speaking is not just restricted to revelation to a prophet.

It does not fail to give the impression that he was spoken to through the intermediary of a prophet who was with him. That would make his kingdom similar to that of Ṭālūt—one of the Israelites—who was advised and guided by their Prophet. The reason for this impression is that God is referred to in the third person.

The clause,you either give them a chastisement or do them a benefit (ḥasanan), means either punish those people or do something of benefit to them. Ḥasanan (benefit) is a verbal noun meant as the subject, taking the place of an implied noun which it describes. Alternatively, it is an adjective for emphasis. In the alternative, it is claimed that making ittikhādh

al-ḥasan (doing them a benefit) the opposite of punishing suggests that it is preferable. It could be a declarative statement of two possibilities meant to indicate that both are permissible. Thus it is a declarative intended as a performative. What it would mean is: It is up to you whether you punish them or forgive them. However, what is likely is that it is interrogative— he is being asked what he is going to do: subjugate or forgive. This last alternative is the best because of the context of the answer which deals with punishment and doing good in different situations, As to him who is unjust, we will chastise him . . . And as for him who believes and does good, he shall have goodly reward. If the clause, you either give them a chastisement or do them a benefit, is a choice between alternative obligations, then,

As for him who believes and does good, would have been an endorsement of it and an announcement of acceptance, which is of little point. In short, it means: “We asked him what he wanted to do to them— punish them or do them good—after defeating them and becoming their ruler. He replied: ‘We will punish whoever of them is a wrongdoer and he will be returned to his Lord and He will punish him with an exemplary punishment. We will be good to pious believers and give them ease.’” The object is not mentioned in, immā an tuʿadhdhiba (lit. either you punish) but it is in, immā an tattakhidha fihim ḥusnan (or you do them a benefit) because they were not all wrongdoers. It is not permissible to apply a punishment meant for people who deserve it to absolutely everyone but it is permissible to be good to the whole of a people among whom

there are good and bad.

8

(18:87) He said: As to him who is unjust, we will chastise him, then shall he be returned to his Lord, and He will chastise him with an exemplary (nukran) chastisement.

The words nukr and munkar mean “unprecedented,” that is, He will give them a punishment without precedent which they had not reckoned on and not expected. Ẓulm has been interpreted by some as “polytheism” and taʿdhīb as “killing.” On the basis of this interpretation, the clause, as to him who is unjust, we will chastise him, would mean, as for him who is a polytheist and does not resile from polytheism, we will kill him. This is the case if “who is unjust” is being contrasted with “who believes and does good”. However the likely reason for the contrast is that being unjust means all of the following: (1) polytheists; (2) those who do not believe in God at all; and (3) those who believe and do not attribute associates to Him but fail to do good, instead making mischief in the land.

If it had not been contrasted to believing, the likely meaning of ẓulm would have been making mischief without any regard to polytheism because the customary practice of kings who were just was to cleanse their land of the mischief made by mischief-makers. Similarly, there is no evidence for chastisement only meaning killing.

8

(18:88) And as for him who believes and does good (ṣāliḥan), he shall have goodly reward (jazāʾan al-ḥusnā) and We will speak to him an easy word (yusran) of Our command (amrina).

The word ṣāliḥan is an adjective which takes the place of an implied noun which it describes. The same is true of al-ḥusnā. Jazāʾ (reward) is: (1) A circumstantial qualifier, with the implied meaning: and as for whoever believes and does good work he will have good reward (al-mathūbat al-ḥusnā) in the circumstance of its being a satisfactory performance of obligation (ḥālli-kawnihimujziyan); or (2) Specifying complement, with the impliedmeaning: whoever believes and does good work he will have good in terms of reward (min ḥayth al-jazāʾ); or

(3) Absolute object, with the implied meaning: We will reward him a reward (nujzihi jazāʾan) (that is, We will reward him greatly).

And We will speak to him an easy word (yusran) of Our command (amrina): The word yusr means that which is easy (maysūr). It is an adjective which takes the place of an implied noun which it describes. The likely meaning of amr is a command pertaining to obligations (amr taklif ). The implied meaning is: “We will say an easy word of Our command to him, that is, We will give him an obligation which is easy for him and not difficult for him.”

(18:89–90) Then he followed (another) course. Until, when he reached the land of the rising of the sun, he found it rising on a people to whom We had given no shelter from it;

That is, then he prepared a means to travel and then traveled toward the eastern horizon until he reached the desert to the east. He then found the sun rising over a nomadic people for whom We had provided no protection from the sun.

Satr, means protection from the sun. It can either be buildings and clothing or buildings only, that is, they lived on the land without having any houses to take refuge in or to protect themselves from the sun. They were also naked, without any clothing. Attributing that to God in the clause, to whom We had given no shelter from it, is an allusion to the fact that they had not yet averted to it, not learned how to build houses, put up tents or weave and sew clothes.

(18:91) Even so! (kadhalika) and We had a full knowledge of what he had.

The likely meaning of kadhalika (even so) is an allusion to the description just given of them. Comparing something to itself—based on the

opinion that in a comparison the thing compared should be different to what it is compared with—renders a somewhat emphatic meaning. There are alternative suggestions for what the demonstrative pronoun “that” (dhalika) in kadhalika (lit. like that) refers to, but they are very different from what is ordinarily understood.

And We had a full knowledge of what he had: The pronoun (“he”) refers to Dhū l-Qarnayn. The sentence (grammatically speaking) is circumstantial. What it means is he adopted a means of travel, reached where the

sun rises, and found such and such a people in a state, full knowledge of which We have. We know all the provision he has, what he will make happen, and what happens to him. It is likely that having full knowledge of what he had is an allusion to Dhū l-Qarnayn’s choice and that he acted through God’s guidance and commandment. He would only come or go out as guided or ordered—as alluded to what was said about his journey to where the sun sets, We said, O Dhū l-Qarnayn! . . .

The verse, that is, and We had a full knowledge . . ., in its allusory meaning is similar to: And make the ark before Our eyes and (according to) Our

revelation. . . (11:37), . . . He has revealed it with His knowledge . . . (4:166),

and . . . and He encompasses what is with them . . . (72:28).

It is also said [that the verse means], (1) To state the greatness of his affair and that God alone has full knowledge of the particulars and minutiae; (2) to embellish what Dhū l-Qarnayn suffered on this journey. The

difficulties and hardships he endured are within God’s knowledge and do not elude Him, or (3) to state the greatness of the course he took. However, the explanation we gave above is better.

(18:92–93) Then he followed (another) course. Until, when he reached (a place) between the two mountains, he found on that side of them a people who could hardly understand a word.

The word sadd means mountain or any other obstruction blocking the way. Thus al-saddayn means two mountains.

He found on that side of them a people, that is, close to the two mountains. The clause, who could hardly understand a word, is an allusion to their simpleness and the superficiality of their understanding. It may be said that it is an allusion to the strangeness of their language and its remoteness from all the languages known to them. That is not an unlikely explanation.

(18:94) They said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn! surely Gog and Magog make mischief in the land. Shall we then pay you a tribute on condition that you should raise a barrier between us and them.

It is likely that those who said this were the people he found between the two mountains. Gog and Magog were two generations of people who came from behind the two mountains and raided them, killing, wounding or pillaging them all. The context provides proof of that because the

pronoun used to refer to them is exclusive to rational beings, the barrier was erected between the two mountains and so on.

Shall we then pay you a tribute (kharajan) . . . : The word kharaj means what is taken from one’s money to spend on things one needs. They made him an offer to give him money in exchange for his erecting a barrier between them and Gog and Magog, to stop them from crossing the barrier and transgressing against them.

(18:95) He said: That in which my Lord has established me (makkanni) is better, therefore you only help me with strength/ workers, I will make a fortified barrier between you and them.

The basis of makkannī (established me) is makkananī but one of the nūns has been blended into the other. A radm is a barrier. Alternatively, it is said that it is a strong barrier. Based on this interpretation, his saying

in response to their request for a sadd (barrier) meant giving them what they wanted and promising what was more than what they needed and expected.

Dhū l-Qarnayn had no need for the tribute they offered him in exchange for his erecting a barrier. He says: “The abundance and strength in which my Lord has established me and settled on me is better than the money you promise me so I have no need for it.”

Therefore you only help me with strength (quwwa): The word quwwa means that through which one has the power to do something. The phrase follows logically from what came of their suggestion to him—their request from him to build them a barrier. In short, it means—as for tribute, I have no need for it, but as for the wall, if you want, help me with what will enable me to build it, for example men and building materials—the examples mentioned were blocks of iron, molten brass, and blowing in the bellows. I will build you a strong barrier.

Thus, it is clear that what they meant by their offer to him of kharaj was the wage for making the barrier.

(18:96) Bring me blocks of iron; until, when he had filled up the space between the two mountain sides, he said: Blow, until, when he had made it (as) fire, he said: Bring me molten brass which I may pour over it.

The word zubar is the plural of zubra just as ghuraf (rooms) is the plural of ghurfa (room). Zubra means block. It is said that sāwa means the same as sawwa (to make two things level). In fact sawwa is an alternative recitation. Al-ṣadafayn is the dual form of ṣadafiwhich is one of the two sides of a mountain. Some say that it can only be said if there is another mountain next to it and parallel to it. It is one of those nouns that only come as part of a pair, for example zawj (spouse or one of a pair), ḍiʿf (half), etc. Qiṭr means copper or molten brass. Ifrāgh means pouring it onto the holes, fiaws and gaps.

Atūnī zubar al-ḥadīd means “bring me blocks of iron” so that I can use them in the barrier. It is part of the quwwa (strength) he asked them for. He may have singled it out for mention and not mentioned stone or any other building materials because it is the main ingredient in building a strong barrier. The phrase, atūni zubar al-ḥadīd (bring me blocks of iron), is substitution of the specific for the general fa aʿinuni bi quwwatin (therefore you only help me with strength/might) or it implies, “He said . . .” This (style) appears frequently in the Qur’an.

Until, when he had filled up the space between the two mountain sides, he said: Blow . . . (Ḥattā idhā sāwā bayn al-ṣadafayni qāla anfukhū): There is brevity in these words through the use of omission and implication. They assisted him with might and brought him what he asked of them so he built them a barrier and erected it

The clause, he said: Blow, is likely that it is an instance of not wanting to mention the dependent object of the verb because it indicates the verb itself. What it means is placing the nozzles of the bellows on the barrier to heat up the iron in it and pour the molten brass onto the cracks and gaps. Until, when he had made it (as) fire. . .: Again implication and brevity are employed. The implied meaning is: “Then he blew until, when he

had made it—that is, what he blew the bellows onto, or the iron—fire, or like fire in terms of its appearance or temperature.” This is an example of metaphorical borrowing (istiʿāra).

He [Dhū l-Qarnayn] said: Bring me molten brass which I may pour over it: This means: “Bring me molten brass which I may empty and pour onto it to block the cracks and make the barrier solid, through which nothing can penetrate.”

(18:97) So they were not able (fa mā sṭāʿū) to scale it (yaẓharūhu) nor could they (wa mā staṭāʿū) make a hole (naqban) in it.

The words isṭāʿū and istaṭāʿū mean the same thing (they are able, negated with mā in the Arabic). Ẓuhūr means being up high and climbing up high. Naqb means the same as thaqb, that is, hole. However, al-Rāghib explains in al-Mufradat fiigharīb al-Qurʾān that a hole in a wall or a skin is called a naqb while a hole in wood is called a thaqb. The plural pronouns refer to Gog and Magog.

There is implication and brevity in these words. The implied meaning is: Then he built a barrier and Gog and Magog were unable to climb

it because it was so high or make a hole in it because it was so strong.

(18:98) He said: This is a mercy from my Lord, but when the promise of my Lord comes to pass He will make it level with the ground, and the promise of my Lord is ever true.

The word dakkāʾ means the same as dakk which is the most severe beating. It is a verbal noun (literally meaning beating flat) but it can be used to mean the same as the object of the verb (that is, beaten flat). Alternatively, it is claimed that it means al-nāqa al-dakkāʾ, that is, a camel which has no hump. Based on this interpretation, it is an example of metaphorical borrowing (istiʿāra). What it means is destruction of the barrier—so people say.

He said: This is a mercy from my Lord, that is, Dhū l-Qarnayn said after building the barrier: “This (the barrier) is a mercy from my Lord, that is, a mercy and protection by which the evil of Gog and Magog are held back from nations of people.”

In the words, but when the promise of my Lord comes to pass He will make it level with the ground, there is omission and implication. The implication is: “This mercy will remain until my Lord’s promise comes. When

my Lord’s promise comes He will make it flat—level with the ground.” The promise means either a promise from Him specific to the barrier— that it will be fiattened close to the Hour, making this is an apocalyptic future prediction related by Dhū l-Qarnayn—or His general promise of the coming of the Hour, which will fiatten mountains and destroy the world. He emphasizes what he says with (the words), and the promise of my Lord is ever true.

9

(18:99) And on that day We will leave a part of them in conflict with another part, and the trumpet will be blown, so We will gather them all together;

It is apparent from the context that the plural pronoun refers to the people. This is supported by the fact that the pronoun “them” in, We will gather them, definitely refers to the people because with plurals, what applies to one instance applies to all.

And on that day We will leave a part of them in conflict (yamūju) with another part: This is metaphorical borrowing.1 It means that on that day, they will be beaten around by the severity of the terror like the swelling of the sea, being pushed against each other. They will lose their order, and disorder and chaos will rule. Their Lord will turn away from them, His mercy will not encompass them and their affair will not be put right by His care.

It is as if the verse fills in the blanks of the clause, but when the promise of my Lord comes to pass He will make it level with the ground. It is

similar to His words elsewhere: Even when Gog and Magog are let loose and they shall break forth from every elevated place. And the true promise shall draw nigh, then lo! the eyes of those who disbelieved shall be fixedly open: O woe to us! surely we were in a state of heedlessness as to this; nay, we were unjust (21:96–97).

In any event, the verse is a prediction of a future apocalyptic event. It has become clear from the above that the word, tark (We will leave) in the verse means what one immediately thinks it does—the opposite of

1 Yamūju means it—that is, the sea—heaves. (Trans.)

taking. There is no need for what some people have said, that is, that tark actually means making (jaʿl), which is one of its antonyms.

The verse constitutes God’s words and is not the end of what Dhū l-Qarnayn said. The proof of that is the shifiifrom the third person to the first person [plural of majesty] addressing another—the same as earlier on, in the clauses, Surely We established him, and, We said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn. If it had been the end of what Dhū l-Qarnayn said, it would have read, “He will leave” in line with, He will make it level with the ground. And the trumpet will be blown: This is the second blow—which resurrects—as evidenced by words, so We will gather them all together; and

the next verse, And We will bring forth hell, exposed to view, on that day before the unbelievers.

(18:101) Those whose eyes were under a cover from My reminder and they could not even hear.

This explains who are meant by the unbelievers. It is between them and remembrance of Himself that God put up a barrier. That is why it is appropriate to talk about their condition after mentioning Gog and Magog. So He put their eyes under a cover from remembrance of Him and took away the power of hearing from their ears. Thus the way between them and the truth—remembrance of God—has been taken away.

The truth can only be reached with one’s sight by looking at God’s words and being guided by them to what they indicate and guide toward, or with one’s hearing through listening to the wisdom, warning, stories, and lessons. Those people have no sight or hearing.

(18:102) What! do then those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants to be guardians instead of Me? Surely We have prepared hell for the entertainment of the unbelievers.

The question is rhetorical. Majmaʿ al-bayān says it means:

“Do those who reject belief in the Oneness of God think that they can take lords instead of Me to help them and stop My punishment from reaching them?”

This implied meaning is evidenced by (the sentence), Surely We have prepared hell for the entertainment of the unbelievers.

There is a second explanation narrated on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, namely that it means:

“What! Do then those who disbelieve think that they can take gods instead of Me and that I will not get angry for My own sake and not punish them?”

A third explanation is that the clause, that they can take, is the first object of ḥasiba which means think. Its second object is implied. The implied meaning is:

“What! Do then those who disbelieve think that their taking servants as guardians instead of Me will be of any avail to them and stop them from being punished.”

The difference between this explanation and the two previous ones is that in the two previous explanations, an (“that”) and its relative phrase take the place of two objects. What is implied is part of the relative phrase. In contrast, according to this third explanation, an (“that”) and its relative phrase is only the first object. The second object is implied.

A fourth explanation is that an (“that”) and its relative phrase take the place of the two objects. The purpose of these words is to deny their ittikhādh (taking) being true ittikhādh, meaning that it is not ittikhādh at all. This is because ittikhādh can only be mutual, that is, both parties taking each other. Those taken disassociate themselves from them because

they say: They shall say: Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not they . . . (34:41).

The four explanations are in descending order of merit, that is, the first one is the best and is supported by the context provided by the verses. These verses and indeed all the verses in the chapter are there to explain that people have been seduced by the embellishment of life in this world. They have become confused and rely on ostensible causes and take others as guardians instead of God. They think that their guardianship will suffice them, avail them, and keep harm at bay. The truth is that what they

will encounter after the trumpet is blown and they are gathered contradicts that because the verse denounces what they think and believe after

that had been their inclination. Next, the need to infer a second implied object is eliminated because the permissibility of an (“that”) and its relative phrase take the place of the two objects of ḥasiba, having done so in

many other places, for example: Nay! do those who have wrought evil deeds think (ḥasiba) that We will make them like those who believe . . . (45:21). This is in spite of the fact that some grammarians have said that it is not allowed.

The chosen interpretation is supported by the subsequent verses, Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in (their) deeds? Similarly, it is supported by the recitation attributed to ʿAlī and several others, a fa ḥasbu, meaning: “What! Is taking My servants as guardians instead of Me enough for them?”

The (plural) word “servants”in the sentence, that they can take My servants to be guardians instead of Me, is any of the angels, jinn, and perfect humans worshiped by idolaters.

Some exegetes say that what is meant by them is the Messiah, the angels, and other favored ones like them, but not shayṭāns because the annexation in this word ʿibādi (My servants) is mainly used to honor that which is annexed.

Author’s reply:

1) The context does not suit honoring, as is obvious.

2) Second, the qualifier min dūni (instead of me) explicitly indicates that “those who disbelieve” means the idolaters who do not worship God in spite of acknowledging His divinity, instead they only worship intercessor associates. As for the People of the Book, for example, Christians take

the Messiah as a guardian but they do not deny God’s guardianship. On the contrary, they attest to both guardianship and then worship them both as one. This is something the reader should understand. Thus, the fact is that ʿibādī (My servants) does not include the Messiah and humans like him. Rather, it is exclusive to the idolaters’ gods. “Those who disbelieve” means the idolaters alone.

Surely We have prepared hell for the entertainment of the unbelievers, that is, something they enjoy when they first arrive in the hereafter.

The hereafter is likened to a home where a guest stays. Hell is likened to entertainment with which a guest is honored when he first arrives. That which comes after two verses adds to the subtlety and beauty of this analogy—that no weight will be assigned to them on the Day of Resurrection.

It is as if they will enter hell immediately. There is obvious scorn in the verse. It is as if it was brought on by the way they scorned [God] in this world, as in the verse, . . . and they mocked My Signs and My messengers.

Examining Narrations

Tafsīr al-Qummī says:

“When God’s Messenger related the account of Moses, his servant, and al-Khiḍr, the people asked him: Tell us about a traveler

who traveled the world, east and west. Who was he? What was his story? Thereafter, God revealed, And they ask you about Dhū l-Qarnayn . . .”

Author’s comment: The details of this oral tradition came up in the discussion on the story of the Companions of the Cave. Something to the same effect is also narrated in al-Durr al-manthūr on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥatim on the authority of al-Suddī and on the authority of ʿUmar—Ghufra’s freeman. The reader should realize that there is amazing discrepancy, contradiction, and incoherence in all the particulars of the story and in all the aspects of the oral traditions about the story of Dhū l-Qarnayn, narrated by both the Shī‘ah and the Sunnī on the authority of the Prophet and, by the Shī‘ah on the authority of the People of the Household, and, similarly the sayings narrated on the authority of the Companions and successors and treated like sacred hadith by the Sunnī. Furthermore, they contain odd things which a sound intellect shies away from, the mind thinks are impossible, and which the real world refutes. A critical researcher would not doubt if he compared them with each other and reflected on them that they are not free of interpolation, fabrication, and astonishing exaggerations in the story’s description. The strangest of them are those narrated on the authority of Jewish scholars who became Muslims, such as Wahb b. Munabbih, Kaʿb al-Aḥbar or those stories within which are clues which give the impression that they are taken from them—so these are of no help to us. They have been narrated wholesale, numerous and long as they are. We shall refer only brief y to some of the ways in which they differ and suffice ourselves with narrating what is mostly free of discrepancy.

One of the differences between them is over his personage. Most of them say that he was human. Others1 say that he was an angel from

1 al-Durr al-manthūr narrates on the authority of al-Aḥwaṣ b. Ḥakīm on the authority of his father on the authority of the Prophet and on the authority heaven whom God sent down to earth “and granted means of access to everything”. Al-Maqrīzī’s Khiṭaṭ says, on the authority of al-Jāḥiẓ’s Kitāb al-ḥayawan [The book of animals], that Dhū l-Qarnayn’s mother was human but his father was an angel.

Another of the differences is over his characteristics. Most narrations say that he was a pious servant who loved God, so God loved him

About the Story of Dhū l-Qarnayn

A Qur’anic and Historical Study Divided into Sections 1. The Story of Dhū l-Qarnayn in the Qur’an His name, the history of the time of his birth, his life, lineage, and all his other particular characteristics are not addressed as was customary in the stories (of the people of) the past. Rather, the Qur’an suffices

itself with mentioning three journeys he made. The first was to the West, until he reached where the sun sets—he found it setting in a black or hot sea and found a people there. His second journey was to the East, until he reached where the sun rises—he found it rising on a people for whom God had not made any shelter. His third journey was to a place between two mountains—he found on that side of them a people who could hardly understand a word. They complained to him about the mischief made in the land by Gog and Magog and offered to pay him a tribute in exchange for his building a barrier between their people and Gog and Magog. He fulfilled their request by building the barrier and promised them that he would build it above their expectations, refusing to take any tribute. He only asked them to help him with parts and labor. In the story, there is reference to men and blocks of iron, bellows, and molten brass.

The particulars and fundamental aspects which can be understood from the story are:

First: That the person the story is about was called Dhū l-Qarnayn before the story in the Qur’an was revealed and indeed even in his lifetime, as is clear from the context: And they ask you about Dhū l-Qarnayn . . .

(18:83). We said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn . . . (18:86). They said: O Dhū l-Qarnayn . . . (18:94).

Second: He believed in God and the Final Day and followed the religion of Truth, as is clear from His words: This is a mercy from my Lord,

but when the promise of my Lord comes to pass He will make it level with the ground, and the promise of my Lord is ever true (18:98). As to him who is unjust, we will chastise him, then shall he be returned to his Lord, and He will chastise him with an exemplary chastisement (18:87). And as for him who believes and does good . . . (18:88).

It adds to his religious standing that His words, either give them a chastisement or do them a benefit, indicate his being supported with revelation, inspiration or one of God’s prophets who was with him to guide

him by communicating the revelation to him.

Third: He was one of those for whom God had brought together all the good of this world and the hereafter. As for the good of this world, it was the mighty kingdom which took him from where the sun sets to where it rises. Nothing stood up to him and all means of access were at his disposal. One of the features of his fortified barrier—in addition to not being in the west or the east—was that it was between two mountains like walls; he filled the space between the two mountain sides and used blocks of iron and molten brass to build it. 3. Who is Dhū l-Qarnayn and Where is his Barrier?

Historians and exegetes have various opinions on the matter depending on their different views on what the story applies to.

(a) Some of them attribute the barrier referred to in the Qur’an is the Great Wall of China between China and Mongolia built by Qin Shi Huang, one of the Chinese Huangs, to stop attacks by the Mongols against China. It is three thousand kilometers long, nine meters wide, and twenty-five meters high. It was built with stone. Building commenced in 264 BCE and it was completed in ten or twenty years. Based on this premise, Dhū l-Qarnayn was the aforementioned Huang.

Comment: This is refuted by the fact that Dhū l-Qarnayn and his barrier’s attributes and characteristics as mentioned in the Qur’an do not apply to this Huang and the Great Wall of China. There is no mention of this Huang’s traveling from his land to the far west. Further, the barrier mentioned in the Qur’an is described as being a fortified barrier (radm) between two mountains. Blocks of iron and qiṭr, that is, molten brass, were used to build it. The Great Wall of China is three thousand kilometers long, stretching along flat land and mountains but it is not between

two mountains. It is built of stone and no iron or molten brass was used to construct it.

(b) Some attribute the builder of the barrier to one of the Assyrian kings.1 In about the seventh century before the birth of Christ, Scythian nations2 would raid from the Caucasus mountain passes to Armenia then in the west of Iran and may even have reached the lands of Assyria, the in the north and the environs of Turkistan in the west.
